text: What AGI means, how it differs from today’s AI, and a practical case study
Opening: This deck uses AGI as a conceptual target, not a claim that it has already been achieved.
A useful working definition focuses on breadth, adaptation, and independence.
AGI describes a hypothetical AI system that can learn and apply knowledge across many domains at a level comparable to a capable human.
Works across unfamiliar tasks, not one narrow workflow.
Uses prior knowledge to solve a new problem with little extra training.
Plans, uses tools, and checks its work against real constraints.
Definition note: There is no universally accepted test for AGI. Treat this as a practical framing for discussion.
Today’s systems can be highly capable without meeting a broad AGI definition.
Detects patterns in a defined task.
Creates and transforms content from prompts.
Pursues a goal through tools and multi-step workflows.
Generalizes across domains and adapts reliably to novelty.
Speaker point: Agentic AI can execute multi-step tasks, but that alone does not establish general intelligence.
Capabilities an AGI system would need
The challenge is not just intelligence in isolation. It is dependable performance in changing environments.
Interpret goals, constraints, uncertainty, and social signals.
Update knowledge without losing prior capabilities.
Apply a method learned in one domain to another domain.
Break goals into steps, use tools, and recover from failure.
Show sources, assumptions, and limits to a human reviewer.
Respect permissions, policies, and risk thresholds.
This slide moves the conversation away from a single benchmark and toward reliable behavior in real workflows.
If systems become broadly capable, they could expand the range of work software can perform. The same capability raises the stakes for oversight.
Coordinate complex work across systems and teams.
Provide expert-level support in more languages and settings.
Confident errors can cause real-world harm.
A powerful system needs clear boundaries and human authority.
Access, bias, and accountability require deliberate design.
Avoid claiming AGI will automatically create these outcomes. Benefits depend on product design, governance, and access.
Illustrative scenario: a health system uses an advanced AI assistant to reduce delays in patient discharge while clinical staff retain every final decision.
Bed status, orders, discharge notes, transport availability
Identify blockers and estimate which patients could leave safely
Draft task lists and route questions to the right teams
Flag uncertainty, conflicting data, or high-risk cases
Human control point: clinicians approve discharge decisions and the system cannot write orders.
Case study is illustrative. It shows how broad reasoning could augment a complex workflow without giving the system autonomous clinical authority.
The assistant acts as a coordinator. Clinical accountability remains with people.
Builds a shared view and identifies blockers
Nurse, physician, case manager validate the plan
Teams complete tasks and update the record
The core design principle: match automation authority to risk. Lower-risk coordination can be more automated than clinical decisions.
How to evaluate a system like this
A convincing demo is not enough. Teams need evidence that the system improves work without creating unacceptable risk.
Does it identify the correct blocker and propose a workable next step?
Does it surface uncertainty and avoid unsupported recommendations?
Does it reduce coordination burden without adding review overhead?
Does performance stay consistent across patient groups and care settings?
Do discharge delays, rework, and escalations improve over time?
Use a staged rollout, a defined baseline, independent review, and clear stop conditions.

AGI is a direction of travel,
not a product category today.
Build useful agents with limits, oversight, and evaluation.
Give AI coordination work first. Keep high-stakes decisions with accountable people.
Discussion: Where would broader AI capability create value in your organization, and where must human authority remain?
Close with the discussion question. Avoid predicting a timeline for AGI; focus on responsible capability building now.
